recent_posts.title: Why we ignore feedback and how to actually use it
recent_posts.summary: Feedback often gets politely acknowledged but never acted upon, stored away like unwanted gifts. The real value of feedback lies in its ability to reveal when we're wrong—but only if we're willing to define what being wrong would look like beforehand. Effective feedback reception requires moving beyond judging whether criticism is "accurate" to understanding what it reveals about how others experience our work. Upward feedback is particularly easy to dismiss, yet it provides irreplaceable perspective from those affected by our decisions. Genuine, honest feedback from people who care isn't freely given—it's earned through consistently responding with curiosity and visible change rather than defensiveness.

recent_posts.title: Teaching real lessons with fake worlds
recent_posts.summary: Building realistic simulations for teaching helps students develop problem formulation and interpretation skills that AI tools can't automate. By creating synthetic worlds with authentic data patterns—including causal correlations, realistic distributions (normal, log-normal, power-law), and temporal rhythms—educators can provide safe environments where students learn to handle messy, real-world technical challenges. The approach uses emergent complexity from simple agent-based rules rather than manually coding every detail, producing datasets that mirror production systems while allowing students to experiment without real-world consequences.

recent_posts.title: If managers were angels
recent_posts.summary: A narrative exploring the challenges of early career software development through the story of Alleigh, a junior developer struggling with a seemingly simple task while navigating poor communication, absent mentorship, and organizational dysfunction. The story illustrates common workplace dynamics including manager burnout, inadequate onboarding, and the gap between technical skills and corporate survival skills, ultimately showing how adaptation and relationship-building become essential for career longevity.

recent_posts.title: The architecture of truth-seeking
recent_posts.summary: Organizations naturally drift toward comfortable fictions rather than uncomfortable truths. Through detailed case studies, this piece examines how well-intentioned teams create elaborate deceptions - from automation systems that don't work to misleading A/B test results. The solution isn't asking individuals to be heroes, but designing organizational structures with equal political standing, interlocked accountability, operational proximity, and protected truth-tellers that make maintaining lies more exhausting than confronting reality.

recent_posts.title: Work Hard, Have Fun, Go Home
recent_posts.summary: Hustle culture prioritizes the appearance of hard work over actual results, creating toxic workplace dynamics that harm both individuals and organizations. The author shares personal experiences showing how strategic thinking and sustainable work practices lead to better outcomes than grinding through long hours. Key warning signs include employees who never take real vacations, single points of failure in critical systems, and leadership that emphasizes effort over results when facing challenges. The most effective teams focus on innovation and value creation rather than time spent at desks.

recent_posts.title: Short-term metrics, long-term harm
recent_posts.summary: Tech companies use A/B testing to optimize for short-term engagement metrics like time spent, which can lead to addictive product features that harm users long-term. The author draws parallels between social media's documented negative effects and emerging concerns about AI chatbots, arguing that optimizing for engagement without considering broader consequences repeats harmful patterns seen in tobacco and processed food industries. The piece advocates for product builders to take responsibility for understanding and mitigating long-term user harm, rather than blindly following metrics that increase engagement.

recent_posts.title: Building adaptable skills in the age of AI
recent_posts.summary: A computer science professor addresses student concerns about LLMs threatening their career prospects. Drawing from personal experience during the dot-com bust and outsourcing fears, he argues that focusing on adaptable, transferable skills rather than specific technologies is key to career resilience. The piece emphasizes developing critical thinking, problem-solving abilities, and communication skills over narrow specialization, comparing career strategy to evolutionary adaptability using a koala versus rat analogy.

recent_posts.title: How to be a better software manager
recent_posts.summary: Software management success comes from building strong teams rather than relying on tools and processes. Key principles include delegating accountability to team members, crafting clear vision based on customer understanding, building trust to reduce unnecessary process overhead, managing complexity through iteration, establishing appropriate planning horizons, measuring meaningful success metrics, and maintaining ethical leadership practices.

recent_posts.title: How daydreaming drives professional success through vision and execution
recent_posts.summary: Daydreaming and visioning are essential for professional success when balanced with execution. Setting aside dedicated time for unstructured thinking helps build direction and purpose in work, preventing reactive decision-making. The key is combining regular dreaming sessions with incremental action steps, creating a cycle where vision and reality inform each other to drive continuous improvement and achievement.

recent_posts.title: Throwaway Code: A Love Story
recent_posts.summary: Throwaway code, initially dismissed as wasteful, becomes a powerful tool for iterative software development. The author explains three stages of iterative development: pretending (surface-level agile adoption), done done (emphasis on completing work within sprints), and customer use (focusing on delivering value to users quickly). The key insight is that software requirements aren't truly known until customers use the software, making short feedback cycles critical. Writing throwaway code intentionally helps launch features early and gather real user feedback, ultimately preventing larger amounts of unused code that result from building off-track features.
